demand-s2.title: Four news items about e-scooter rentals in Porthaven
demand-s2.html:
Porthaven is an invented city where riders rent e-scooters by the trip. A local paper ran four items in one month:

  1. The rental company raised its price per trip from $3 to $4.
  2. The city raised bus fares by 50 cents.
  3. A survey found that riders expect the rental price to jump next month.
  4. A factory closed, and many residents earn less. Riders who can afford a car or a bike tend to stop renting scooters.

supply-s2.title: Four events for the furniture workshops of Larkfield
supply-s2.html:
Larkfield is an invented town where small workshops make wooden chairs. Four things happen over one year:

  1. A storm closes forests in the region and the price of lumber jumps.
  2. Workshops start using a new laser cutter that halves the time it takes to shape each chair.
  3. The town starts paying each workshop $20 for every chair it produces.
  4. Workshop owners hear that chair prices will rise sharply next month.

price-elasticity-demand-s2.title: Three goods at an island general store
price-elasticity-demand-s2.html:
The only store on Tallis Island, an invented place reached by a weekly ferry, sells three goods among many others:

  • Insulin, which some islanders need every day and which has no substitute on the island.
  • Fizzle, one of six brands of sparkling water on the shelf, all of which taste much the same.
  • Table salt, which costs about $1 a box and lasts a family a month.

The store manager raises the price of Fizzle by 10% and sees the quantity of Fizzle sold fall by 30%.

disequilibrium-changes-s2.title: Olive oil in Teralia: two news items in one season
disequilibrium-changes-s2.html:
Teralia is an invented country with a large market for olive oil. In one season:

  1. A long drought ruins much of the olive harvest, so presses have fewer olives to work with.
  2. A widely reported medical study finds that olive oil is good for the heart, and many families decide to cook with it.

No other news affects the market.

trade-policy-s3.title: Varrow opens its wheat market
trade-policy-s3.html: Varrow, an invented small country, has not traded wheat with other countries. Inside Varrow, wheat sells for $180 a ton. The government removes its ban on trade. Wheat sells on the world market for $240 a ton, and Varrow is too small for its sales to change that price.

items.q: Label the axes and the curve of a market demand graph for concert tickets.
The price of printer ink rises sharply. Ink and printers are used together. Shift the right curve in the market for printers.

key.because: a rise in the price of a complement (ink)

slips.S: The price of ink changes what buyers of printers want, not the cost of making printers, so it shifts demand, not supply.

items.q: A town of 20,000 people grows to 30,000 as new families move in. Shift the right curve in the town's market for haircuts.

slips.S: New residents are buyers of haircuts; the number of buyers is a demand shifter.

mistakes.why: That uses the starting values (20 cases, $8). The midpoint method divides each change by the average: 30 cases and $7.
That puts the price change on top. Divide the percent change in quantity by the percent change in price.

options: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>%</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>income</mtext><mo>÷</mo><mo>%</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%\Delta \text{income} \div \%\Delta Q_d</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>%</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>÷</mo><mo>%</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>income</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%\Delta Q_d \div \%\Delta \text{income}</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>%</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>÷</mo><mo>%</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%\Delta Q_d \div \%\Delta P</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>spending</mtext><mo>÷</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>income</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta \text{spending} \div \Delta \text{income}</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: The cross-price elasticity of demand between printers and ink cartridges is <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1.2</annotation></semantics></math>. What are the two goods?
options: Substitutes
Unrelated goods
Inferior goods
Complements

items.q: Why must you keep the sign for income and cross-price elasticity but read the absolute value for price elasticity of demand?
options: Their sign tells the type of good or relationship; price elasticity's sign does not
Income and price changes are positive, so their elasticities are too
Price elasticity of demand is larger, so its sign is dropped
The sign shows whether demand is elastic

items.q: The income elasticity of demand for ski trips is 1.8. Incomes rise by 5%. What happens to the quantity of ski trips demanded, other things equal?
options: It rises by about 1.8%
It falls by about 9%
It rises by about 9%
It rises by about 3.6%

items.q:
A researcher estimates these elasticities for a good called Brisk bars. Which statements follow? Select all that apply.
Income elasticity: −0.3-0.3. Cross-price elasticity with Crunch bars: +0.8+0.8. Cross-price elasticity with milk: −0.5-0.5.
options: Brisk bars are an inferior good
Brisk bars and Crunch bars are complements
Brisk bars and milk are complements
Demand for Brisk bars is price inelastic

items.q: A rise in the price of gasoline lowers the quantity of large trucks bought. What does this say about the cross-price elasticity of demand for large trucks with respect to the price of gasoline?
options: It is positive, so the goods are substitutes
It is negative, so the goods are substitutes
It is zero, so the goods are unrelated
It is negative, so the goods are complements

items.q: What are the equilibrium price and quantity of kelp bars?
options: $3 and 70 bars
$5 and 80 bars
$4 and 60 bars
$6 and 100 bars

items.q: Calculate consumer surplus in the kelp bar market at equilibrium, in dollars per day.

mistakes.why: That is a rectangle. Consumer surplus is a triangle, so take one half: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>×</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tfrac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 6</annotation></semantics></math>.
That uses the price, $4, as the height. The height is the gap from the price up to where demand starts: $10 minus $4.

items.q: Calculate producer surplus in the kelp bar market at equilibrium, in dollars per day.

mistakes.why: That is a rectangle. Producer surplus is a triangle: take one half.
That measures down to $0. Supply starts at $1, so the height is $4 minus $1.

items.q: Calculate total surplus in the kelp bar market at equilibrium, in dollars per day.

mistakes.why: That forgets the one half in each triangle.
That subtracts producer surplus from consumer surplus. Total surplus adds them.

items.q: In the graph, which area is consumer surplus?
options: Area a
Area b
Areas a and b together
The area to the right of the equilibrium quantity

items.q: In the graph, which area is producer surplus?
options: Area a
Areas a and b together
The area under the supply curve
Area b

items.q: Suppose sellers produced more than the equilibrium quantity and found buyers for the extra units only by charging less. Compared with total surplus at equilibrium, total surplus would be
options: larger, because more units are traded
smaller: those units cost more than they are worth
the same, because the gains and losses cancel
larger, because buyers pay a lower price

items.q: Shade consumer surplus at the market equilibrium.

slips.ps: That area lies above supply and below the price: producer surplus. Consumer surplus is under demand.

items.q: Shade producer surplus at the market equilibrium.

slips.cs: That area lies under demand and above the price: consumer surplus. Producer surplus is above supply.

items.q: Shade total surplus at the market equilibrium.
Supply of a good has increased to the curve shown. Shade consumer surplus at the new market equilibrium.
Mark the market equilibrium on the graph.
What is market equilibrium?
options: The price at which sellers earn the most profit they can
The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
The highest price any buyer would pay for the first unit
The quantity at which the government sets prices

items.q: Four buyers would pay at most $10, $8, $6 and $4 for one concert poster each. Posters sell for $5 each. What is the total consumer surplus of the buyers who buy, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That counts the $4 buyer, who does not buy at $5 and so gains nothing (not minus $1).
That adds what each buyer would pay. Consumer surplus is what they would pay minus the price, for those who buy.

items.q: A farmer would sell a bushel of apples for as little as $12 and sells it for $20. What is the farmer's producer surplus on that bushel?
A frost cuts the coffee harvest and the price of coffee rises. Coffee growers in other regions plant more coffee trees, and some cafes switch to tea. What role is the higher price playing?
options: A signal steering growers and buyers
A cost that shifts demand for coffee to the right
A price that growers set and buyers accept
A sign that the market has stopped working

items.q: Which statements about total surplus at the equilibrium of a competitive market are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus
It is as large as it can be at the equilibrium quantity
It equals the price times the quantity traded
It rises if sellers produce beyond the equilibrium quantity

items.q: At a price of $30, is there a shortage or a surplus of helmets, and how large is it? Give the size of the gap in helmets.

mistakes.why: That adds the two quantities. A shortage is the gap: quantity demanded minus quantity supplied.
That is the quantity supplied. The shortage is how far it falls short of the 70 demanded.

items.q: If the price of helmets starts at $30, what happens next, and why?
options: The price falls toward $20 as sellers clear their stock
Demand shifts left until it meets supply at $30
The price rises toward $40 as buyers compete for too few helmets
The price stays at $30 because 40 helmets are sold

items.q: At a price of $60, what is the size of the gap between the quantities, in helmets?

mistakes.why: That adds the two quantities. A surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded.
That is the surplus at $50. Read the $60 row.

items.q: Helmet laws spread, and buyers now want 30 more helmets at each price in the table. What are the new equilibrium price and quantity?
options: $50 and 80 helmets
$40 and 90 helmets
$60 and 70 helmets
$40 and 60 helmets

items.q: What does the drought alone do to the market for olive oil in Teralia?
options: Demand decreases: price and quantity fall
Supply decreases: price and quantity both fall
Supply increases: price falls and quantity rises
Supply decreases: price rises and quantity falls

items.q: With both news items together, what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity of olive oil?
options: The price and the quantity both rise
The price rises; the change in quantity is indeterminate
The quantity falls; the change in price is indeterminate
The price rises and the quantity falls

items.q: An economist later finds that the shift in demand was much larger than the shift in supply. What happened to the equilibrium quantity of olive oil?
options: It fell
It rose
It stayed the same
It is still indeterminate

items.q: A popular video makes padel, a racket sport, a craze. Shift the right curve in the market for padel rackets and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a change in tastes toward padel

slips.S: The video changes what buyers want, so demand shifts; racket makers' costs did not change.

items.q: A cheaper chip lowers the cost of making smartwatches. Shift the right curve in the market for smartwatches and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a fall in the price of an input

slips.D: A cheaper chip lowers the cost of making watches, so supply shifts, not demand.

items.q: In the market for e-bikes, incomes rise (e-bikes are a normal good) and a new battery design cuts production costs. Shift both curves and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: higher incomes and lower production costs

items.q: A frost destroys half the wheat crop, and wheat is the main input for bread. Nothing changes for bread buyers. Shift the right curve in the market for bread and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a rise in the price of an input (wheat)

items.q: At a price below the equilibrium price, which is true?
options: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus
Demand shifts left to meet supply
The market clears at the lower price
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage

items.q: In a kelp bar market, demand reaches zero at $10 and supply starts at $1, with equilibrium at $4 and 60 bars a day. Demand rises: the new demand curve reaches zero at $13, and the new equilibrium is $5 and 80 bars. By how many dollars does consumer surplus change?

mistakes.why: That is consumer surplus after the change. Subtract the $180 before to get the change.
That forgets the one half in each triangle.

items.q: In the same kelp bar market, by how many dollars does producer surplus change when the equilibrium moves from $4 and 60 bars to $5 and 80 bars?

mistakes.why: That is producer surplus after the change; subtract the $90 before.
That is the change in consumer surplus. Producer surplus lies above supply and below the price.

items.q: Demand for two goods rises by the same amount. Good X has very inelastic supply; good Y has very elastic supply. Which statement is correct?
options: The price of X rises more than the price of Y
The quantity of X rises more than the quantity of Y
The price of Y rises more than the price of X
Both prices rise by the same amount

items.q: Supply of a good decreases while demand stays the same. Which results are certain? Select all that apply.
options: The equilibrium price rises
The equilibrium quantity rises
Consumer surplus rises
The change in price is indeterminate

items.q: Demand for umbrellas falls and supply of umbrellas rises at the same time. Which change is certain?
options: The quantity falls; price is indeterminate
The price rises; quantity is indeterminate
The price falls; quantity is indeterminate
Both price and quantity fall

items.q: In the graph, a per-unit tax is collected from sellers. Which areas together are the government's tax revenue?
options: Areas c and e
Areas b, c, d and e
Areas b and d
Area a

items.q: In the graph, which areas are the deadweight loss of the tax?
options: Areas c and e
Areas b and d
Area f
Areas a and f

items.q: In the graph, which area is consumer surplus after the tax?
options: Areas a, b and c
Areas a and b
Areas a and c
Area a

items.q: In the graph, demand and supply are equally steep. How is the burden of the tax shared?
options: Sellers bear the whole tax, because they hand it over
Equally: area b for buyers and area d for sellers
Buyers bear the whole tax, because the price rises
Buyers pay area c and sellers pay area e

items.q: At the Halden rent ceiling of $900, how large is the shortage of apartments?

mistakes.why: That compares quantity demanded with the old equilibrium quantity. The shortage compares quantity demanded with quantity supplied at $900.
That is how far the quantity rented falls (3,200 to 2,500). The shortage is 4,000 minus 2,500.

items.q: How many apartments are rented in Halden under the ceiling?
Who gains and who loses from Halden's rent ceiling?
options: Renters as a group gain from the lower rent, and landlords lose
Landlords gain, because scarce apartments are easier to rent out
No one loses, because renters now pay a lower rent
Renters who find a unit gain; landlords and renters left out lose

items.q: Over several years, landlords in Halden convert some apartments to condos for sale and build few new rentals. What happens to the shortage at the $900 ceiling?
options: It grows, as fewer rentals are offered at $900
It shrinks, as rents rise to $1,200
It disappears, as renters move away
It stays at 1,500, as the ceiling is unchanged

items.q: Calculate the government's daily revenue from the kombucha tax, in dollars.

mistakes.why: That uses the quantity before the tax. Only the 800 cans still sold are taxed.
That is what buyers spend after the tax. Revenue is the tax per can times the cans sold.

items.q: What percent of the tax do buyers bear?

mistakes.why: That is the sellers' share: the fall in the price they keep, $0.20 of the $1 tax.
Sellers hand the tax to the government, but buyers pay only $0.80 more. The rest comes out of the price sellers keep.

items.q: What do the kombucha results say about the elasticities in this market?
options: Supply is less elastic than demand
Demand and supply are equally elastic
Demand is less elastic than supply
Demand is perfectly elastic

items.q: Calculate the deadweight loss of the kombucha tax, in dollars per day.

mistakes.why: That is a rectangle. The deadweight loss is a triangle, so take one half.
That is the tax revenue, which goes to the government and is not lost.

items.q: Draw a binding price ceiling on the graph.

slips.Pc: A ceiling above the equilibrium price does not bind: the market price is already lower, so nothing changes.

items.q: Draw a binding price floor on the graph.

slips.Pf: A floor below the equilibrium price does not bind: the market price is already higher.

items.q: The government places a per-unit tax on sellers of the good. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a per-unit tax collected from sellers

slips.D: The tax is collected from sellers, so it shifts supply. (A tax collected from buyers would shift demand left, with the same result.)

items.q: The government pays sellers a per-unit subsidy. Shade the cost of the subsidy to the government.

slips.dwl: That triangle is only the deadweight loss. The cost is the whole rectangle between the two prices out to the new quantity.

items.q: A per-unit subsidy is paid to sellers. Shade the deadweight loss it creates.
A binding price ceiling is in place. Shade the deadweight loss.
A binding price floor is in place. Shade consumer surplus.
Before a subsidy, 50 units are sold. The government pays sellers $2 for each unit, and the quantity sold rises to 60. What is the cost of the subsidy to the government, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That uses the quantity before the subsidy. The government pays on all 60 units sold after it.
That counts only the 10 extra units. The subsidy is paid on every unit sold.

items.q: In a market with equilibrium $5 and 50 units, a price ceiling of $3 is set. At $3, 30 units are supplied, and buyers would pay up to $7 for the 30th unit. Calculate the deadweight loss, in dollars.

mistakes.why: That is a rectangle; take one half.
That uses the gap from the ceiling to the equilibrium price, $2. The height is the gap between demand and supply at 30 units: $7 minus $3.

items.q: A city sets a ceiling of $2.50 on a bus ticket when the market price is $2.00. What happens?
options: A shortage, because a ceiling holds the price down
The price rises to $2.50
A surplus, because sellers want to charge $2.50
Nothing: the ceiling is above the equilibrium price

items.q: A government limits the number of fishing licenses, so the yearly catch of a fish falls from the market quantity of 900 tons to 600 tons. Other things equal, what happens in the fish market?
options: The quantity falls to 600 tons and the price falls
The price stays the same because demand is unchanged
The quantity falls to 600 tons and the price rises
The quantity rises because each boat fishes more

items.q: The government gives sellers a $1 subsidy for each unit. Compared with before, what happens to the prices buyers pay and sellers receive?
options: Buyers pay more and sellers receive less
Buyers pay less and sellers receive more
Buyers pay $1 less and sellers receive the same
Both prices stay the same and quantity rises

items.q: A binding price floor is set for milk. Which results follow? Select all that apply.
options: A surplus of milk
More milk is bought than before
The price buyers pay falls
Consumer surplus rises

items.q: In the graph, the country imports at the world price plus a tariff. Which area is the government's tariff revenue?
options: Areas d and f
Areas b and c
Area e
Areas d, e and f

items.q: In the graph, which areas are the deadweight loss of the tariff?
options: Areas d and f
Area e
Areas b and c
Area a

items.q: In the graph, which areas make up domestic producer surplus with the tariff?
options: Area g
Areas e and g
Areas a, b and c
Areas b, c and g

items.q: In the graph, how much consumer surplus do buyers lose when the tariff is added to the world price?
options: Area e
Areas b, c, d, e and f
Areas d and f
Areas b and c

items.q: Dornia opens to trade at the world price of $3. How many tons of rice does it import per day?

mistakes.why: That is all the rice Dornians buy. Domestic farms still supply 30 tons; imports are the gap.
That is the gap at $4. Read the $3 row.

items.q: Dornia adds a tariff of $1 a ton, so rice now sells in Dornia for $4. How many tons does it import per day?

mistakes.why: That is the import level at the world price. At $4 domestic supply is higher and quantity demanded lower.
That is the quantity demanded at $4; subtract the 40 tons Dornian farms supply.

items.q: How much revenue does the $1 tariff raise per day, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That uses imports before the tariff. The tariff falls only on the 20 tons still imported.
That taxes all the rice bought in Dornia. Only imports pay the tariff.

items.q: Without trade, Dornia's rice market clears at $5 and 50 tons. By how many dollars per day does total surplus in Dornia rise when it opens to trade at $3, with no tariff?

mistakes.why: That is a rectangle; the gain from trade is a triangle, so take one half.
That is the rise in consumer surplus alone. Producer surplus falls by $80, so total surplus rises by $40.

items.q: Once Varrow opens to trade, what happens in its wheat market?
options: The price falls and Varrow imports wheat
The price rises to $240 and Varrow exports wheat
The price stays at $180 and Varrow sells abroad
The price rises to $240 and Varrow imports wheat

items.q: Who in Varrow gains and who loses when it opens to trade in wheat?
options: Wheat buyers gain; wheat farmers lose
Both farmers and buyers gain
Both farmers and buyers lose
Wheat farmers gain; wheat buyers lose

items.q: What happens to total surplus in Varrow's wheat market after it opens to trade?
options: It rises: producers gain more than consumers lose
It falls: consumers lose more than producers gain
It does not change: the gains and losses cancel
It rises by exactly what consumers lose

items.q: A small country opens its market and will import the good. Draw the world price on the graph.

slips.PW: A world price above the domestic equilibrium price would make the country an exporter.

items.q: A small country imports at the world price, with no tariff. Shade consumer surplus.

slips.cs-before: That is consumer surplus without trade; at the lower world price it is larger.

items.q: A country exports at a world price above its domestic equilibrium price. Shade domestic producer surplus.
A tariff is added to the world price. Shade the tariff revenue.

slips.dwl: Those triangles are the deadweight loss; the revenue is the rectangle between them.

items.q: A tariff is added to the world price. Shade the deadweight loss of the tariff.
Instead of a tariff, Dornia allows only 20 tons of rice imports a day (an import quota). Compared with free trade at $3, what happens?
options: The price stays at $3 and imports fall to 20 tons
The price falls because fewer imports compete
The price rises to $4 and imports fall to 20 tons
Imports rise because the quota guarantees 20 tons

items.q: Why does a country that opens to trade import a good whose world price is below its own price?
options: Domestic farms are forced to stop producing
The government sets the world price below the domestic price
Imports raise the domestic price
Other producers make it at a lower opportunity cost

items.q: A small country that imports a good adds a tariff. Which group gains from the tariff? Select all that apply.
options: Domestic buyers of the good
Domestic producers of the good
Foreign sellers of the good

items.q: How does a tariff on imports compare with an import quota that allows the same amount of imports?
options: A quota lowers the domestic price; a tariff raises it
A tariff creates a deadweight loss, but a quota does not create one
Same price and imports; only a tariff gives the government revenue
A quota raises imports above free trade; a tariff lowers them
